newsitem.title: USA: U.S. praises PLO statements against terrorism.
newsitem.headline: U.S. praises PLO statements against terrorism.

text.p: The United States praised Palestinian leaders on Friday for moving against extremists and said the PLO had made a "clear statement" against terrorism -- a key condition for reviving stalled peace talks.

Speaking as Palestinian negotiators held a second day of talks at the State Department, spokesman Nicholas Burns said there were positive signs of growing security cooperation between the Palestinians and Israel.

Acclaiming the "very specific assurances" that Secretary of State Madeleine Albright received on Thursday from the Palestinians, Burns said subsequent remarks by negotiator Saeb Erekat were "a very clear statement renouncing terrorism".

Erekat said the PLO acknowledged "that peace and violence don't go together, and as Palestinians we do not condone or tolerate the killing of Israelis." He said the Palestinian Authority would continue efforts to stop violence.

Street battles have flared in the West Bank nearly every day since Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, on March 18, sent bulldozers to start work on a Jewish housing project on an East Jerusalem hill.
Israel has said it will not resume peace talks, stalled since January, until the violence stops. The Palestinians say their condition for resuming is that Israel stops work on the housing project.

Burns said Washington had now seen reports of the Palestinian Authority taking measures against extremists, working with the Israelis to identify a guerrilla cell in Gaza and collaborating with them to oppose violence in Hebron.
"So we are beginning to see some re-emergence of security cooperation between the two, and that is quite positive," he told a news briefing.

Albright on Friday telephoned Mahmoud Abbas one of the Palestinian negotiators in Washington. The Palestinian team later visited the State Department for talks and lunch with Middle East envoy Dennis Ross.
Over the past week the United States has put to the Palestinians, and to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, a set of ideas for reviving the peace process.
Although it has not disclosed the ideas, they are believed to include a Palestinian crackdown on violence and terrorism and Israeli restraint in building in disputed areas.

Burns called on both sides to "reflect very seriously" on the ideas, predicted further contacts with them over the weekend and said the United States expected to able to decide its next steps by early next week.
The U.S. spokesman reiterated that the Israeli-Palestinian talks remained at an impasse for the moment. He had cautioned on Thursday that no breakthrough appeared imminent.

Despite speculation about possible Middle East trips by Ross or Albright, Burns said no decisions had been made "as of this moment" for either to go there. He said Washington was considering all options, however.
